channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Zillow removed climate risk scores. This climate expert is restoring them.
item.description: Ars Technica: “Zillow removed the feature displaying climate risk data to home buyers in November after the California Regional Multiple Listing Service, which provides a database of real estate listings to real estate agents and brokers in the state, questioned the accuracy of the flood risk models on the site. Now, a climate policy expert in California is working to put data back in buyers’ hands.”

item.title: YouTube, TikTok, and Adobe are bringing creators to Sundance. Here’s what to watch for.
item.description: Tubefilter: “Social media content creators are becoming Sundance fixtures as they take new roles both behind and in front of film cameras. Tech companies have supported that trend by using Sundance as an opportunity to introduce internet standouts to the broader entertainment industry.”

item.title: I use this advanced search engine to find specific apps the Play Store tries to bury
item.description: MakeUseOf: “After years of scrolling past half-answers and off-target suggestions, I stumbled onto App Finder. It’s not really a Google Play Store alternative. Rather, it’s an independent search engine that indexes the Play Store’s database but gives you the controls Google removed.”

item.title: Why Sydney is preserving thousands of flowers after deadly Bondi attack
item.description: BBC: “Plastic sheeting is taped across all the windows and there’s a large padlock hanging on the door handle. Step inside, though, and you’re greeted by cuddly toys, candles, trinkets and messages of hope scribbled on large sheets. All of them come from a makeshift memorial that was created after the 14 December attack at Bondi Beach that killed 15 people.”

item.title: “Does this channel have more juice in it?” YouTuber J.J. McCullough on a “sustainable” life as a news creator
item.description: NiemanLab: “When J.J. McCullough first started making YouTube videos in 2015, he was 31, and worried he was too old to break through on an already saturated platform. McCullough had lost his job as a political commentator on the conservative Canadian TV channel Sun News Network when the station abruptly shut down. ‘I bought a little camcorder at Best Buy,’ he said, and decided to give YouTube a try.”

item.title: Judge Sides Against Google In Search Users’ Antitrust Suit
item.description: MediaPost: “Google search users can proceed with an antitrust suit over the company’s search deals with Apple and others, a federal judge ruled this week.”

item.title: Google and Epic Games struck a secretive $800 million deal, ‘helping Google market Android’
item.description: 9to5 Google: “As revealed in the ongoing court saga, Google and Epic Games have apparently struck a new deal that involves Android, Unreal Engine, and some sort of ‘product development,’ and it’s going to remain a secret for the time being.”

item.title: This Berkeley professor is exposing the hidden physical toll of our digital world
item.description: Berkeley News: “In her forthcoming book, Earthy Algorithms: A Materialist Reading of Digital Literature, [Professor Alex] Saum-Pascual argues that digital tools like generative AI mask the messy reality of the internet — the massive energy, hardware and human labor it requires — to trick us into thinking we are separate from nature.”

item.title: Measuring US workers’ capacity to adapt to AI-driven job displacement
item.description: Brookings Institution: “While definitions vary, studies using exposure measures seek to estimate the extent to which AI systems can help complete the work tasks of different jobs. But these measures are not predictions of job displacement. Rather, they provide signals about where AI’s complex labor market effects are most likely to emerge first. However, most exposure-focused analyses overlook a critical dimension: workers’ ability to adapt if job loss does occur.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Guinness Adverts Project on Irish Film Institute’s Archive Player
item.description: Irish Central: “The Guinness Archive partnered with the Irish Film Institute’s (IFI’s) Irish Film Archive to catalog, digitize, and preserve a collection of more than 500 16mm and 35mm advertisements, making it the largest publicly available collection of brand advertising in Ireland and the UK.”

item.title: Got Ideas For Growing The Open Social Web? Bring Them.
item.description: Techdirt: “Johannes Ernst from FediForum and I are doing something about it. On March 2nd, we’re hosting an online ‘un-workshop’ focused on one question: how do we actually grow the open social web even more? And, yes, I’m on the board of Bluesky, but this isn’t Bluesky specific. We want an open discussion and brainstorming on growing the wider open social web.”

item.title: The Taylorsville Times Highlights New Years Resolutions
item.description: DigitalNC: “Thanks to funding from our partners at Alexander County Library, new issues of The Taylorsville Times (Taylorsville, N.C.) are now available on our website! These editions, published from 1997 to 2010, highlight local events, sports, and major news.”

item.title: Google begins offering free SAT practice tests powered by Gemini
item.description: Ars Technica: “Of course, generative AI can go off the rails and provide incorrect information, which is a problem when you’re trying to learn things. However, Google says it has worked with education firms like The Princeton Review to ensure the AI-generated tests resemble what students will see in the real deal. The interface for Gemini’s practice tests includes scoring and the ability to review previous answers.”

item.title: eBay updates legalese to ban AI-powered shop-bots
item.description: The Register: “eBay has decided to ban agentic shopping bots from its digital tat bazaar. The company’s decision emerged in an update to its user agreement posted on January 20th, which insists users must not use ‘buy-for-me agents, LLM-driven bots, or any end-to-end flow that attempts to place orders without human review’ on the site, unless eBay grants approval.”

item.title: AYF Olympics Analytics Project: Modernizing nearly a century of athletic history
item.description: Armenian Weekly: “The AYF Central Executive is pleased to announce the ongoing AYF [Armenian Youth Federation] Olympics Analytics Project, an initiative designed to strengthen the preservation, accessibility and long-term management of AYF Olympic historical data.”

item.title: The White House Confirms It Altered Photo of Arrested Protester to Depict Her Sobbing: ‘The Memes Will Continue’
item.description: Mediaite: “The White House has confirmed that it posted a fake arrest image of a Minnesota protester to its official X account Thursday.”

item.title: Researchers say they convinced Gemini to leak Google Calendar data (updated)
item.description: Mashable: “Researchers with the app security platform Miggo Security recently released a report detailing how they were able to trick Google’s Gemini AI assistant into sharing sensitive user calendar data (as first reported by Bleeping Computer) without permission. The researchers say they accomplished this with nothing more than a Google Calendar invite and a prompt.”

item.title: Evidence for link between digital technology use and teenage mental health problems is weak, our large study suggests
item.description: The Conversation: “After following more than 25,000 young people in Greater Manchester over three school years, we found little evidence that self-reported time spent on social media or frequent gaming causes mental health problems in early-to-mid adolescence. Instead, the relationship between digital technology use and teenagers’ wellbeing is far more nuanced than simple cause and effect.”

item.title: Grok could have produced 3 million sexual deepfakes in 11 days, says estimate
item.description: Politico: “A study on the artificial intelligence chatbot Grok embedded on X estimates it created 3 million sexualized images in 11 days in January, including 23,000 of children. Meanwhile European regulators have yet to decide how to handle the explosion of nonconsensual deepfakes on the already embattled platform.”

item.title: Built To Lie: How New Pro-Russian Monuments Exploit Cultural Heritage
item.description: StopFake: “Russia’s foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) operations are diverse, entrenched, well-resourced, and coordinated. They are also linked globally to culture through ‘Cultural Heritage Exploitation’, or CHX. CHX is a multi-institutional endeavour with spatial, temporal, cognitive, and material aspects.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: ‘Sports Illustrated’ Launches Branded ‘SI TV’ FAST Channel
item.description: Media Play News: “Sports Illustrated, the 70-year-old media platform, Jan. 20 announced the launch of ‘SI TV,’ a free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) channel available on myriad platforms. The channel aims to bring the brand’s legacy storytelling to a video platform, featuring original programming, live events, sports lifestyle and archival content.”

item.title: OpenAI moves on ChatGPT ads with impression-based launch
item.description: Search Engine Land: “According to a report, OpenAI is already testing ads with select advertisers and plans to charge on a pay-per-impression (PPM) basis, rather than the more familiar pay-per-click model. The test is expected to be limited, with advertisers committing under $1 million each and no self-serve buying tools available yet.” Ah yes, just what the Internet needs, more ad space.

item.title: YouTube CEO promises more AI features in 2026
item.description: Engadget: “In a lengthy blog post outlining YouTube’s 2026 plans, CEO Neal Mohan said the company will continue to embrace this new ‘creative frontier’ by soon allowing its creators to throw together Shorts using their AI-generated likeness.” Gross!

item.title: The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture: Anti-ICE Protests on Roblox
item.description: Lifehacker: “Recently, in response to ICE protests in Minnesota, Roblox users have been staging their own demonstrations within the game. Led by @clipsforcloset, users are reenacting ICE raids, holding up signs, and otherwise expressing their deep feelings about current events.”

item.title: Apple is reportedly working on an AI pin wearable that is AirTag-sized
item.description: Mashable: “Apple is getting into the AI wearable space with its very own AI pin, according to a new report from The Information. According to the report, Apple’s AI pin could be released as soon as 2027 and would be around the size of a slightly thicker AirTag.”

item.title: Millions of people imperiled through sign-in links sent by SMS
item.description: Ars Technica: “Websites that authenticate users through links and codes sent in text messages are imperiling the privacy of millions of people, leaving them vulnerable to scams, identity theft, and other crimes, recently published research has found.”

item.title: Protecting Yourself from Phishing Scams on Flickr
item.description: Flickr Blog: “We’ve recently seen an increase in malicious phishing scam messages targeting Flickr members through FlickrMail and comments, often impersonating Flickr staff. Here’s what you need to know to recognize these scams and respond safely.”

item.title: Why light-weight websites may one day save your life
item.description: Marijke Luttekes: “Sites should load on crappy internet connections and on older devices, and respect browser and system-wide accessibility settings, and several device input methods (mouse, keyboard, voice, among others). I do not see as much talk about website performance and size as I would.”

item.title: Global app spending overtakes mobile games for the first time as AI assistants fuel growth
item.description: TechSpot: “Sensor Tower’s annual State of Mobile report shows that global consumers spent around $167 billion on apps in 2025. The new record figure marks a 10.6% year-on-year increase.”

item.title: 4 smartphone sensors you can experiment with in the Physics Toolbox app
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Beneath the surface, every smartphone is packed with specialized sensors that support the features you use every day. These sensors are typically hidden from smartphone users, handling both obvious and obscure use cases. Something as simple as a microphone might be used for calls and voice recordings, but also serve double duty to provide loud noise warnings. You can unlock every sensor inside your phone with the free Physics Toolbox app.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: https://localsearchamerica.com/local-news-tv/
item.description: We’re about to get whomped by an ice storm but issues will continue as long as the power stays on. If you’d like to check local news coverage of the weather, check out Local News TV, part of Local Search America: Local News TV offers YouTube feeds from 660 TV stations in America, organized by state and DMA (metro area, sorta.) Filters available for topics including weather.

item.title: Andrew Anderson Has Compiled an Online Archive of the Detroit Legend Ron Signs
item.description: New-to-me, from Print: “In time, [Andrew Anderson] identified the artist as Ron Miller, and put his collection of about 250 Google Street View screenshots of his signs dating back to 2009 on his website. He also created a virtual Ron Signs map plotting out all of them throughout the city, and published a Twitter thread to share his findings that began to amass attention around Detroit and beyond.”

item.title: Search Bench
item.description: Spotted on Hacker News: From the announcement: “I built Search Bench as a small experiment to compare search engines without showing which engine produced which results. It was inspired by the idea behind the LLM Arena, but applied to search.” I did two searches, one with a common word (cows) and one with a much rarer word (agrivoltaics). The cow query was a close choice but I ended up choosing Google’s results over Brave’s. The agrivoltaics query was no contest and I quickly chose Google’s results over Bing’s.

item.title: Data centers are now the fastest-growing part of US construction
item.description: TechSpot: “New data from FMI Corp., a Raleigh-based construction forecasting firm, shows spending on data center construction will climb 23% in 2026, even as office, hotel, apartment, and warehouse development slows sharply. That growth will bring the sector’s share of total nonresidential building to more than 6%, compared with just 2% three years ago.”

item.title: As YouTube refreshes its look, is it time to say goodbye to the play button?
item.description: Tubefilter: “YouTube’s previous redesigns have drawn criticism, so the desire to avoid overstimulating users is a prudent choice. But after testing its latest refresh for months, the official rollout is a bit underwhelming. The shift is so subtle that some users might not even notice a difference.” Sounds good to me!

item.title: I rebuilt my Windows setup using only free open-source apps
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I decided to rebuild my Windows setup using only free open-source apps. The goal wasn’t simply to find Microsoft 365 alternatives. I was building a different system and trying to break free from the Microsoft ecosystem to whatever extent possible, while still using Windows 11.”

item.title: Comic-Con Bans AI Art After Artist Pushback
item.description: 404 Media: “… anti-AI sentiment is growing in the artistic community and an artist-led backlash against Comic-Con’s AI-friendly language led to the convention quietly changing the rules.”

item.title: Trump administration says DOGE may have misused Social Security data
item.description: NBC News: “The Justice Department alerted a federal judge in Maryland that members of the Department of Government Efficiency working with the Social Security Administration may have misused data it obtained from that agency.”

item.title: Canada is looking to ban kids under 14 from using social media: report
item.description: Mobile Syrup: “Following recent moves made by Australia, the Government of Canada is looking to ban social media services for kids under 14 as part of an upcoming ‘online harms bill,’ as three sources told The Globe and Mail. The U.K. is also considering Australia’s example.”

item.title: Could ChatGPT convince you to buy something? Threat of manipulation looms as AI companies gear up to sell ads
item.description: The Conversation: “As a security expert and data scientist, we see these examples [of AI-adjacent advertising] as harbingers of a future where AI companies profit from manipulating their users’ behavior for the benefit of their advertisers and investors. It’s also a reminder that time to steer the direction of AI development away from private exploitation and toward public benefit is quickly running out.”

item.title: CSUN Students’ Work Laying Groundwork for National Database on Water Quality Following SoCal’s Major Fires
item.description: San Fernando Sun: “What they learn will go into a national database to help researchers better understand the impact the 2025 fires had on critical environmental characteristics, such as water turbidity. The database will serve as a baseline of information that can be used for future research.”

item.title: Introducing the Myaamia Heritage Foundation
item.description: Aacimotaatiiyankwi: “The Myaamia Heritage Foundation (MHF) is a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization established by the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma. The MHF furthers the Tribe’s cultural mission by promoting and funding research that advances Myaamia cultural knowledge, supporting Myaamia artists and scholars, and providing educational opportunities for both Myaamia citizens and the broader public.”

item.title: Computer History Museum Launches Digital Portal to Its Vast Collection
item.description: Computer History Museum: “The Computer History Museum (CHM), a leader in decoding technology—its computing past, digital present, and future impact on humanity—announced the launch of OpenCHM, a new digital portal providing global access to its unparalleled collection.”

item.title: Race against time: Digital effort saves Khamyang Language; spoken by just one surviving person
item.description: DY365: “AASU and the Nanda Talukdar Foundation have taken a significant step in preserving Assam’s linguistic heritage by digitally archiving three endangered languages: Khamyang, Tai Phake, and Singpho.”

item.title: Organic search traffic is down 2.5% YoY, new data shows
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Organic search traffic is down just 2.5% year over year — nowhere near the 25% to 60% drops often cited in industry commentary. That’s one big takeaway from a new large-scale analysis by Graphite using Similarweb data from more than 40,000 of the largest U.S. websites.”

item.title: How to Turn Your Favorite Tech Blogs into a Personal Podcast
item.description: freeCodeCamp: “I took a few tech blogs I already enjoy reading, picked the best articles, converted them to audio using my own voice, and turned the result into a private podcast. Now I can stay up to date while walking, running, or driving. In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to build a simplified version of that pipeline step by step.”

item.title: Why Everyone Should Still Use an RSS Reader in 2026
item.description: Lifehacker: “It’s now the norm to check social media or the front pages of many different sites to see what’s new. But I think RSS still has a place in your life: Especially for those who don’t want to miss anything or have algorithms choosing what they read, it remains one of the best ways to navigate the internet.” Agreed! I have a whole website full of free tools for finding and creating RSS feeds: https://rssgizmos.com/. Try Kebberfegg for making keyword-based feeds.

item.title: Grok’s Leering Pictures Are the Newest Version of an Old Problem
item.description: Mother Jones: “And now, of course, there’s Grok, the generative AI tool created by Elon Musk’s X, which has been embroiled in a scandal over users using its new graphics-editing feature to create gross images of women—and, crucially, to put those manipulated images on Twitter, where other people can see them, because attempted public humiliation is the goal.”

item.title: Unsealed: Spotify Lawsuit Triggered Anna’s Archive Domain Name Suspensions
item.description: TorrentFreak: “Spotify and several major record labels, including UMG, Sony, and Warner, have taken legal action against the unknown operators of Anna’s Archive. The action follows the shadow library’s announcement that it would release hundreds of terabytes of scraped Spotify data. Unsealed documents reveal that the court already issued a broad preliminary injunction, ordering hosting companies, Cloudflare, and domain name services, to take action.”

item.title: Parents in the UAE now have a legal obligation to monitor children’s digital usage, experts say
item.description: The National (Middle East): “The federal decree law establishes a national Child Digital Safety Council, to be governed by the Ministry of Family, and applies to internet service providers and digital platforms, whether operating within or targeting users in the UAE. It also applies to anyone responsible for the care of children, including parents, redefining obligations regarding digital safety.”

item.title: Century-old solar records refine future cycle forecasts
item.description: Space Daily: “An international team of astronomers has developed a new way to extract solar polar magnetic information from more than a century of historical observations, improving prospects for predicting future solar cycle activity.”

item.title: Turning over a new leaf: Macquarie’s rare plant collection goes digital
item.description: Macquarie University: “A new Atlas of Living Australia grant will help digitise 16,000 plant specimens at Macquarie University, filling critical gaps in national biodiversity data and making rare species records accessible to researchers worldwide.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: TrumpCensorship.com
item.description: Spotted on Bluesky: From the About page: “Whether through the suppression of scientific research, the erasure of inconvenient historical truths, the rewriting of history, or the direct targeting of media organizations, the administration’s actions represent a full-scale attack on democratic norms and the foundational principle of free speech in the United States. The American Sunlight Project started cataloguing these actions early in Trump’s second term, and has visualized them for the public to see the depth and breadth of the continued assault on their First Amendment rights.”

item.title: ICE becomes one of the most-blocked accounts on Bluesky after its verification
item.description: TechCrunch: “ICE (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) has now become the No. 3 most-blocked account on Bluesky, after receiving its official verification on Friday, according to third-party trackers.”

item.title: Meta is *still* running thousands of ads for AI nudifiers
item.description: Indicator: “Despite promising to crack down on such ads in June of last year, the company has failed to stop the flow, according to the latest audit by Indicator. I identified at least 4,431 nudifier ads that have appeared across Meta’s platforms since December 4. The ads promise to turn any photo into a pornographic video and point to 13 different websites and 6 apps.”

item.title: Google temporarily disabled YouTube’s advanced captions without warning
item.description: Ars Technica: “Google has now posted a brief statement and confirmed to Ars that it has not ended support for SRV3. However, all is not well. The company says it has temporarily limited the serving of SRV3 caption files because they may break playback for some users.”

item.title: Russia to Launch AI-Powered Internet Censorship System in 2026
item.description: Mezha: “In 2026, Russia plans to launch a system for censoring internet traffic using artificial intelligence, with 2.27 billion rubles allocated for it…. In 2025 alone, the number of blocked materials rose by nearly 60% – to 1.29 million.”

item.title: Court rules TikTok Canada can continue to operate — for now
item.description: Politico: “A federal court has overturned a Liberal government order to shut down TikTok Canada’s business operations, ordering Industry Minister Mélanie Joly to take another look at the app that more than 14 million Canadians use.”

item.title: AI company Eightfold sued for helping companies secretly score job seekers
item.description: Reuters: “Eightfold AI, a venture capital-backed artificial intelligence hiring platform used by Microsoft, PayPal and many other Fortune 500 companies, is being sued in California for allegedly compiling reports used to ​screen job applicants without their knowledge.”

item.title: Groups targeted by federal hate laws quietly scrub social media channels and website
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Neo-Nazis and Hizb ut-Tahrir have wiped their social media of offensive content as new hate laws pass parliament. The former leader of the National Socialist Network has coached ex-members how to avoid attracting the attention of authorities. A neo-Nazi-linked church has suggested it remains protected by religious freedom laws.”

item.title: New research decodes hidden bias in health care LLMs
item.description: Northeastern News: “Large language models contain racial biases that factor into their recommendations, even in clinical health care settings. Northeastern researchers found a way to reveal these racial associations in LLMs.”

item.title: Does llms.txt matter? We tracked 10 sites to find out
item.description: Search Engine Land: “We wanted data, not debates. So we tracked llms.txt adoption across 10 sites in finance, B2B SaaS, ecommerce, insurance, and pet care — 90 days before implementation and 90 days after.”

item.title: Majority of CEOs report zero payoff from AI splurge
item.description: The Register: “More than half of CEOs report seeing neither increased revenue nor decreased costs from AI, despite massive investments in the technology, according to a PwC survey of 4,454 business leaders.”

item.title: We Need Diverse Books launches Unbanned Book Network to fight school bans
item.description: Associated Press: “A grassroots organization founded to increase diversity in publishing is launching a program to counteract the nationwide wave of bannings in schools and libraries.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: From Stone to Digital: The online Archive celebrating Pinuccio Sciola’s genius
item.description: Panini Cultura News: “The Foundation bearing his name has presented the Pinuccio Sciola Digital Archive, a project that makes the artist’s entire documentary, visual, and design heritage available online.”

item.title: World-leading literature database celebrates 25 years
item.description: University of Queensland: “A dynamic literary database managed by The University of Queensland is celebrating 25 years of preserving Australian literature. AustLit contains digital records of more than one million works and 200,000 authors, managed by a dedicated team at UQ’s St Lucia campus.”

item.title: OpenAI says its mystery AI wearable is on track for 2026 as AI earbuds rumors spread
item.description: Mashable: “Last year, OpenAI announced that it was partnering with legendary iPhone designer Sir Jony Ive to release an AI wearable device, and a company leader recently confirmed the mystery device is on track to ‘unveiled’ by the end of the year.”

item.title: Twin Cities small business owners say Amazon’s AI lists their products without consent
item.description: Minnesota Star Tribune: “Many small business owners are discovering their own products are sold by Amazon through word of mouth or on social media. Others figure it out when orders come in under strange-looking email addresses that lead back to Amazon. In some cases, the practice is causing logistical problems for businesses — such as when AI makes a mistake. [Emily] Johnson said Amazon described one of her silver rings as gold.”

item.title: Ukraine to share wartime combat data with allies to help train AI
item.description: Reuters: “Ukraine will establish a system allowing its allies to train their artificial intelligence models on Kyiv’s valuable combat data collected throughout the nearly ‍four-year war with Russia, newly appointed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has said.”

item.title: Portugal Bans Polymarket Over €4M Insider Trading Scandal
item.description: Cryptonews: “Portugal bans Polymarket after suspicious betting patterns saw over €4 million wagered during the presidential election as odds shifted dramatically two hours before official results, raising insider trading concerns over leaked exit polls.”

item.title: FTC says it will appeal Meta antitrust decision
item.description: Associated Press: “The Federal Trade Commission said Tuesday it will appeal the November ruling in favor of Meta in its antitrust case against the social media giant. The FTC said it continues to allege that, for more than a decade, Meta Platforms Inc. has ‘illegally maintained a monopoly’ in social networking through anticompetitive conduct ‘by buying the significant competitive threats it identified in Instagram and WhatsApp.'”

item.title: AI fails at freelancer tasks 97% of the time, new ‘Remote Labor Index’ shows
item.description: ZDNet: “‘While AI systems have saturated many existing benchmarks, we find that state-of-the-art AI agents perform near the floor on [Remote Labor Index],’ the researchers revealed. ‘The best-performing model achieves an automation rate of only 2.5%. This demonstrates that contemporary AI systems fail to complete the vast majority of projects at a quality level that would be accepted as commissioned work.'”

item.title: 10 things I learned from burning myself out with AI coding agents
item.description: Ars Technica: “Since November, I have used Claude Code and Claude Opus 4.5 through a personal Claude Max account to extensively experiment with AI-assisted software development (I have also used OpenAI’s Codex in a similar way, though not as frequently). Fifty projects later, I’ll be frank: I have not had this much fun with a computer since I learned BASIC on my Apple II Plus when I was 9 years old.”

item.title: UCF Researcher Creates Color-Changing, Tunable Photonic Material Inspired by Nature
item.description: University of Central Florida: “Debashis Chanda, a researcher and professor at UCF’s NanoScience Technology Center, has developed a new material that can change color dynamically in response to external stimuli like temperature, which creates a new possibilities for materials and devices to respond, adapt and be reconfigured in real time.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New Collection in DRI – The National Herbarium of Ireland digital collection of Irish plants
item.description: Digital Repository of Ireland: “The complete collection contains some 20,000 samples of plant products, including fruits, seeds, wood, fibres, plant extracts, and artefacts. At present, the National Herbarium of Ireland digital collection in the DRI Repository has digitally preserved over 5,000 images containing scaled photographs of herbarium specimens collected in Ireland.”

item.title: New ICE Tracking Apps Find Place on Google Play Store Again
item.description: Android Headlines: “New ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) tracking apps, like ICEbreaker and Eyes Up, have emerged on the Google Play Store. These replace the previous enforcement-tracking tools, which were blocked. The apps provide crowdsourced alerts about nearby reported ICE activity.”

item.title: World’s largest database of historic vines nears 9,500 vineyards
item.description: Press Democrat: “The Old Vine Registry, the world’s largest database of landmark vineyards, is approaching 9,500 listings, nearing its goal of 10,000 vineyards by June 2027…. Searchable by country, region, vineyard name, grape variety and more, the registry’s website provides a remarkable look at many of the world’s most venerable vines.”

item.title: How to find reference photos for (almost) every feather
item.description: Found Feathers: “Curious about your favorite bird’s feathers? Ever gotten a feather ID with no proof? Want artistic references for a specific type of feather? This guide may be for you! Read on to learn how I source reference photos for all my feather-related needs.”

item.title: These Are the Best Price-Tracking Tools I Use As a Deals Writer
item.description: Lifehacker: “As a shopping and deals writer, that is what I do for a living, and I know how time-consuming it can be. Luckily, you don’t have to figure it all out yourself: Here are the best websites and extensions I’ve been using for years to check price history and track prices so that you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible.”

item.title: UK exposed to ‘serious harm’ by failure to tackle AI risks, MPs warn
item.description: The Guardian: “Consumers and the UK financial system are being exposed to ‘serious harm’ by the failure of government and the Bank of England to get a grip on the risks posed by artificial intelligence, an influential parliamentary committee has warned.”

item.title: Social media addiction’s surprising challenger? Anti-doomscrolling influencers
item.description: Associated Press: “Yokubonis is a content creator who goes by the name Olivia Unplugged online, making videos to combat overuse or mindless use of social media. For the most part, people who view her videos welcome the disruption from the endless loop of content, treating it as a wake-up call to get off their phones. Other times, they are snarky.”

item.title: Snap reaches settlement in social media addiction lawsuit
item.description: TechCrunch: “According to the New York Times, the settlement was announced Tuesday in the California Superior Court in Los Angeles County. The lawsuit against Snap was brought by a 19-year-old known in court documents as K.G.M., accusing the social media app of designing algorithms and features that caused addiction and mental health issues.”

item.title: Heritage agency files complaint against Kim Keon Hee over private use of cultural sites
item.description: Korea Times: “The Korea Heritage Service (KHS) filed a criminal complaint against Kim Keon Hee, the wife of former President Yoon Suk Yeol, with Seoul’s Jongno Police Station, Wednesday, following an internal audit that found state-managed cultural heritage sites and resources were allegedly used for private purposes.”

item.title: What is happening to Mongolian language and culture online in China?
item.description: PEN America: “More than six million Mongolians living in China are having their culture, language, and identity ripped away from them by the repressive policies and actions of the Chinese government. ‘Save Our Mother Tongue’: Online Repression and Erasure of Mongolian Culture in China, is a new, in-depth report that looks at what happens when a community’s digital rights are violated.”

item.title: Musk claims Tesla will restart work on its Dojo supercomputer
item.description: Engadget: “Elon Musk posted on X that Tesla will be restarting work on Dojo3, the third generation of its in-house supercomputer project. The Dojo team had been disbanded last year as the company prioritized the AI chips that run on board Tesla vehicles. Musk said the company is returning to the project ‘now that the AI5 chip design is in good shape.'”

item.title: New Study Examines Gender Differences in Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence Risk
item.description: Caltech: “A new study, which draws on survey data from approximately 3,000 respondents in the United States and Canada, finds that women, on average, exhibit greater skepticism toward artificial intelligence (AI) technologies than men. Analysis suggests that differences in risk orientation and exposure help explain this gender gap.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: One month after the Epstein files deadline, only a fraction of the DOJ’s records have been released
item.description: NBC News: “Monday marks one month since the deadline for the Justice Department to release all its files related to Jeffrey Epstein, but only a fraction of the records have been made public.”

item.title: Major charities leave X after AI images controversy
item.description: Civil Society: “Major charities including the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) have stopped posting on social media platform X due to controversy surrounding its artificial intelligence tool’s image-creating function.”

item.title: Deep reading can boost your critical thinking and help you resist misinformation – here’s how to build the skill
item.description: The Conversation: “As a cognitive scientist and a literacy expert, we research the ways people process information through reading. Based on our work, we believe that deep reading can be an effective way to counter misinformation as well as reduce stress and loneliness. It can be tough to go deeper than a speedy skim, but there are strategies you can use to strengthen important reading skills.”

item.title: I tried vibe coding an app as a beginner – here’s what Cursor and Replit taught me
item.description: ZDNet: “Startups such as Cursor, Replit, Lovable Labs, Harness, Windsurf, Augment Code, All Hands AI, and Microsoft, with its Visual Studio with GitHub Co-pilot, all offer programs that can drastically reduce the hand-coding humans need to do. And so I wondered: Could a newbie like me, with limited programming knowledge, talk my way through creating an app?”

item.title: NFL-Related Accounts on Facebook Are Posting Some of the Most Shameless AI Slop Yet
item.description: Gizmodo: “There’s a group of accounts on Facebook that claims to be a bunch of fan accounts for various National Football League teams. But a quick scroll through these pages, each sporting a couple thousand followers, reveals misinformation paired with a series of seemingly AI-generated photos. Based on the comment sections of these photos and the amount of likes some of them get, people are fully believing what they post.”

item.title: Meta overlooks illegal online gambling ads, says UK watchdog
item.description: Bloomberg: “Meta Platforms Inc. is turning a blind eye to illegal gambling sites that advertise on Facebook and Instagram, according to the UK’s Gambling Commission. The regulator has been checking Meta’s searchable ad library for operators that don’t have a license but are targeting people in the UK, according to a speech by executive director Tim Miller, delivered at the ICE gaming conference in Barcelona on Monday.”

item.title: NY lawmakers propose domestic violence offender database
item.description: PIX11: “A database could soon track repeat domestic violence perpetrators in New York, thanks to new legislation. State Sen. Mario Mattera and Assemblymember Anil Beephan both introduced legislation this month to create the database. The database would be publicly available and include any person convicted of at least two domestic violence offenses.”

item.title: Building the world’s first open-source quantum computer
item.description: University of Waterloo: “Researchers from the University of Waterloo’s Faculty of Science and the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) are prioritizing collaboration over competition to advance quantum computer development and the field of quantum information. They are doing this through Open Quantum Design (OQD), a non-profit organization that boasts the world’s first open-source, full stack quantum computer.”

item.title: Am I too stupid to vibe code?
item.description: Garbage Day: “Vibe coding, like every new trend coming out of Silicon Valley, turns this process — the entire act of creativity, itself — into a slot machine. One more pull on the AI and maybe it will figure it out for you. You won’t understand how any of it works, of course, or feel particularly proud of what you’ve done, but maybe you’ll have something. Just a few more dollars for some more tokens. C’mon, just pay a bit more.”

item.title: Türkiye’s conservation labs revive thousands of ancient artifacts
item.description: Hürriyet Daily News: “Ministry of Culture and Tourism is conducting extensive conservation and restoration work in its specialized regional laboratories, where experts meticulously preserve and restore historical artifacts — including those repatriated from abroad, damaged by time or recently discovered — to safeguard Türkiye’s rich cultural heritage for future generations. Across the country, 12 restoration and conservation laboratories have so far treated more than 251,000 artifacts.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Just the Browser claims to tame the bloat without forking
item.description: The Register: “Just the Browser is a new project by developer Corbin Davenport. It aims to fight the rising tide of undesirable browser features such as telemetry, LLM bot features billed as AI, and sponsored content by a clever lateral move. It uses the enterprise management features built into the leading browsers to turn these things off.”

item.title: Wikipedia inks AI deals with Microsoft, Meta and Perplexity as it marks 25th birthday
item.description: Associated Press: “Wikipedia unveiled new business deals with a slew of artificial intelligence companies on Thursday as it marked its 25th anniversary. The online crowdsourced encyclopedia revealed that it has signed up AI companies including Amazon, Meta Platforms, Perplexity, Microsoft and France’s Mistral AI.” If you want to try a different way of using Wikipedia which doesn’t involve AI, try WikiTwister.

item.title: Data shows half of all crypto tokens have gone dark, and 2025 was the worst year yet
item.description: TechSpot: “A CoinGecko analysis shows that more than half of all cryptocurrencies ever created have already failed. Of the 20+ million tokens launched between mid-2021 and the end of 2025, 53% are no longer traded, their contracts still float in block explorers but are effectively lifeless.”

item.title: A no-AI icon for humans to use
item.description: CKN: “I have added a tiny… symbol in the footer of my website. It’s supposed to be as unremarkable as a © symbol (though I think we can all agree it basically holds no value whatsoever these days), but communicates that A.I…. will not be found anywhere on here.”

item.title: Call for AI rules after fake video of mayor made
item.description: BBC: “A fake video of a city council mayor has prompted calls for more stringent rules around the use of AI videos in politics. The video at the centre of the row appeared to show mayor Ashley Bowkett saying he would not allow councillors to investigate the ‘missing £8m this year’ and then laughing at the camera.”

item.title: CSWR acquires work of renowned Hollywood writer/director and alumnus Brian Levant
item.description: University of New Mexico: “Brian Levant, a renowned Hollywood filmmaker and UNM alumnus in the College of Fine Arts, has donated his extensive career-long body of work in the entertainment industry to The University of New Mexico’s Center for Southwest Research and Special Collections (CSWR).”

item.title: ‘NVIDIA Contacted Anna’s Archive to Secure Access to Millions of Pirated Books’
item.description: TorrentFreak: “NVIDIA executives allegedly authorized the use of millions of pirated books from Anna’s Archive to fuel its AI training. In an expanded class-action lawsuit that cites internal NVIDIA documents, several book authors claim that the trillion-dollar company directly reached out to Anna’s Archive, seeking high-speed access to the shadow library data.”

item.title: UK ministers launch consultation on whether to ban social media for under-16s
item.description: The Guardian: “Ministers have launched a consultation into whether to ban under-16s from using social media as part of a package of measures designed to curb mobile phone use among young people.”

item.title: Sycophantic chatbots inflate people’s perceptions that they are “better than average”
item.description: PsyPost: “Results of three experiments indicate that sycophantic AI chatbots inflate people’s perceptions that they are ‘better than average’ on a number of desirable traits. Furthermore, participants viewed sycophantic chatbots as unbiased, but viewed disagreeable chatbots as highly biased. The paper was published as a preprint in PsyArXiv.”

item.title: From Paginā to Webpage: On Developing and Documenting a Digitized Latin Collection
item.description: Journal of Open Humanities Data: “In this work, we present three Zenodo repositories related to the creation of digital editions for Latin texts. The first is the Notre Dame Digitized Latin Collection (NDDLC), which contains over 550,000 words of Latin in TEI-XML. ”

item.title: Meet Veronika, the tool-using cow
item.description: Ars Technica: “Her owner, Witgar Wiegele, is an organic farmer and baker who keeps the cow as a pet. With Wiegele’s permission, they conducted a series of randomized trials with a deck scrub broom, chosen for its asymmetrical shape, placed in different orientations. The pair recorded 76 instances of Veronika using the broom over seven sessions of ten trials.” Good morning, Internet…
